transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-08-03 16:00 PDT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Ana Ruiz (Redwood CS), Lena Ortiz (Osprey Head of ML), Marcus Hale (Platform Eng), Priya Kapoor (Security), Evan Lo (Product)

Summary (auto): quick demo of JSON mode and tool-calling; discussed guardrails, canaries, and security posture; agreed next steps and pilot scoping.

00:00 - 00:22 Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya, I'm the AE on this account. Samir will run through the demo, Ana's here to help with pilot logistics. How's everyone doing?
00:23 - 00:48 Lena (Osprey): Good, thanks. We had a quick sync internally, want to see how typed outputs and tool calls could reduce downstream parsing pain, and ensure we don't hallucinate actions that touch payments.
00:49 - 01:15 Samir (Redwood): Great, that's exactly what we'll cover — JSON mode, schema enforcement in the Console, and how the runtime enforces field types and does fallback to safe outputs. Quick ask before we start: do you have a strict schema already or you want us to propose one?
01:16 - 01:35 Lena: We have a rough contract for trade signal payloads, it's a mix of numbers, enums, and nested metadata. We need deterministic outputs, so schema enforcement is big.
01:36 - 02:05 Marcus (Osprey): Also latency requirements: sub-200 ms p95 for inference on core signals, and cost is a concern if this scales. We prefer dedicated infra if it helps with SLOs.
02:06 - 02:40 Samir: Understood. We'll show both hosted and Dedicated patterns. In Console you'll see a 'JSON mode' toggle that enforces typed responses against a provided JSON schema; the runtime will validate and, if necessary, trigger a structured fallback or a second-pass refinement.

03:10 - 03:45 [screen share starts, slight audio echo for a moment]
03:46 - 04:12 Samir: Ok screen share — this is the Console. Top-left route config: you can pin a model and attach a schema. Here's a sample schema for a trade signal: "signal_id" string, "score" number, "action" enum [buy,sell,hold], "confidence" number between 0 and 1, and an optional "explain" object.
04:13 - 04:50 Lena: Nice. How strict is the enforcement? If the model outputs "buy" but with upper-case BUY or misspells, does it auto-normalize?
04:51 - 05:25 Samir: There's a normalization layer — we recommend canonical enums but the runtime can apply configurable normalizers. If it can't reconcile, we can fail the response and trigger a fallback policy: either return a structured error or call a recovery chain (e.g., ask model to regenerate with the schema).
05:26 - 06:05 Marcus: And for throughput, what's the batching story? If we have 100 QPS with short sequences, is batching going to blow up latency?
06:06 - 06:40 Samir: Redwood Optimize suggests batching profiles based on your distribution. For low-latency paths we keep very small batch sizes and leverage per-request routing to low-latency nodes. You can also reserve Dedicated pools — that gives predictable throughput and you can force single-request execution for critical fast paths.

06:50 - 07:30 Priya (Osprey): Security wise we need to know data residency and encryption at rest. Also whether KV caches persist any PII, and how KMS integrates.
07:31 - 08:00 Ana (Redwood): We have SOC2 docs and KMS integration. By default hosted keeps ephemeral caches and customer data is encrypted with customer-managed keys in Dedicated/Private deployments. We'll send the SOC2 + architecture note after this call.

08:20 - 09:10 Samir: Back to tooling — now demonstrating an API call in JSON mode. This is a two-step sequence: 1) provide the schema, 2) issue the payload prompt. You can also attach a 'tool map' — mapping actions in the schema to internal tools (e.g. trade-exec API) and add guardrails so only certain fields permit side-effectful calls.
09:11 - 09:55 Evan (Osprey): That guardrail bit — can we whitelist exact predicates? We want rules like "only execute trades if confidence > 0.9 and action != hold and not flagged_by_risk".
09:56 - 10:25 Samir: Exactly. We demo a policy editor in Console where you build boolean rules referencing schema fields. The runtime evaluates the policy before allowing a tool call; if it fails, it returns the structured decision payload instead of calling the tool.

10:50 - 11:30 [slight crosstalk]
11:31 - 12:05 Samir: I'm going to trigger a failing case: model outputs "BUYY" and 0.95 confidence. The schema validator flags the enum mismatch — our fallback policy here asks the model to re-generate constrained to the schema and if it still fails, we return "requires_human_review" type output.
12:06 - 12:45 Lena: Good — we want that human-in-loop for borderline cases. Do you track lineage/audit for which model version generated the decision and which fallback was used?
12:46 - 13:10 Samir: Yes, each response includes token-level traces, model version, and which guardrail fired. Console has a per-route timeline and a trace link to drill into the sequence. Those are retained per your retention policy and included in Dedicated/Private SLAs.

13:50 - 14:30 Marcus: For private deployment, how invasive is the runtime — do we need to open ports or do you push an agent into our VPC?
14:31 - 15:20 Ana: For Private we ship a customer-managed control plane with connectivity options. You can either host the inference plane in your VPC or we can run in a partner-hosted environment with a private peering link. We'll share the topology diagrams.
15:21 - 16:00 Priya: And HSM? If we require HSM-backed KMS, is that supported for Dedicated/Private?
16:01 - 16:35 Samir: Yes, you can bring-your-own-KMS/HSM and we integrate with common providers; there are some provisioning steps for Dedicated. We'll include the HSM integration notes in the compliance packet.

16:50 - 18:05 [demo — live schema editing]
18:06 - 18:45 Samir: Now a quick live run: sending a batch of three prompts to show typed outputs and the fallback for one bad response. You'll see how the console marks the failing item and returns a structured diagnostic with a code and suggested regeneration.
18:46 - 19:20 Lena: I appreciate that diagnostic — any way to auto-run a quick repair chain before escalating to human?
19:21 - 19:55 Samir: Yes — you can configure automated retry patterns up to N attempts with different temperature or stricter sampling settings, or route to a higher-quality model variant for that item.

20:30 - 22:00 Marcus: Cost math — what's the delta between hosted and dedicated per-token with quantization and the batching we discussed? We need a ballpark to model TCO.
22:01 - 22:40 Maya: I'll send a sample cost model after this call. Optimize includes suggestions like dynamic quantization + KV cache lifetimes that can reduce per-token costs substantially; numbers vary with your seq lengths. For short inference sequences we often recommend int8 quantization and lightweight caching.
22:41 - 23:10 Lena: Does quantization affect accuracy for our risk thresholds? We can't degrade trade decision fidelity.
23:11 - 23:50 Samir: There's a trade-off. Optimize runs a small sweep to recommend model/quantization combos for given prompt sets, and flags any observed regressions on your eval set. For mission-critical signals you can pin to higher-precision models for the critical route and use quantized variants on secondary signals.

24:30 - 25:15 Evan: On the API side, can we have typed responses stream while still enforcing the schema? Some of our UIs like live dashboards need streaming.
25:16 - 25:55 Samir: Streaming with schema is supported — we validate progressively. If later tokens would violate the schema we abort and emit a structured error token. There's also tooling to materialize partial typed outputs for client-side assembly.

26:40 - 28:00 [Customer asks about failure modes and observability]
28:01 - 28:45 Samir: Observability: per-token latency histograms, per-model error rates, and a guardrail dashboard showing policy-fire counts. You'll be able to correlate a spike in structural errors to a model rollout and roll back.
28:46 - 29:20 Lena: Can we run canary rollouts? We want to test model variants incrementally.
29:21 - 30:00 Samir: Yes, Console supports canary percentages at route level with automatic rollback on quality regressions tied to your evals. You can also set a fallback model to take traffic if the primary becomes unhealthy.

30:30 - 31:05 Priya: For audits we need immutable logs and ability to export traces into our SIEM.
31:06 - 31:42 Ana: We export audit logs and traces via secure S3 or a direct ingestion path; we can also push to Splunk/Datadog. We'll include the exact log schema in the docs.

32:10 - 33:00 [Live Q&A — minor delay when Samir switches windows]
33:01 - 34:20 Marcus: One more question around KV cache — we want to persist some metadata for latency; does KV cache ever leak across tenants?
34:21 - 34:55 Samir: No cross-tenant leakage; caches are scoped to customer and route. In Dedicated/Private you can choose cache persistence policy; for PII we recommend ephemeral caches and encrypt at rest with customer keys.

35:40 - 37:00 [Demo wraps up — recap]
37:01 - 37:35 Maya: Quick recap: we showed JSON mode, schema enforcement, guardrails for tool calling, canaries and observability, and Optimize recommendations. Agreed pilot: Osprey provides prompt bank and success metrics; Redwood runs a benchmark and proposes capacity/pricing.
37:36 - 38:10 Lena: Timeline — we'd like a pilot that can run within two weeks; is that realistic?
38:11 - 38:50 Maya: Yes, if we get the prompt bank and access to a test endpoint we can run a scoped pilot in 7–14 days. We'll scope an initial bench of 10k requests/day with the key routes.

39:20 - 41:00 [Negotiation on scope]
41:01 - 42:15 Priya: One blocker is we need an NDA addendum for security docs and a signed DPA. How do you handle that?
42:16 - 42:55 Ana: We have a standard DPA and can do an NDA addendum. I'll attach the templates and a checklist for what we need.

43:30 - 45:00 [Small side discussion about team-resourcing and contacts]
45:01 - 45:40 Samir: For the benchmark, I'll need sample sequences, typical token lengths, and the success criteria you want measured — latency p95, decision accuracy, and rollback tolerance.
45:41 - 46:10 Lena: We'll send that over. Also want to include a few edge-case prompts that test hallucination and ambiguous inputs.
46:11 - 47:00 Maya: Great — so action items captured. Anything else?
47:01 - 47:25 Evan: Just one ask — sample code in Python and Node for typed-output API calls.
47:26 - 47:50 Samir: We'll include both in the repo I'll share.
47:51 - 48:30 Priya: Final — do you have references for financial customers or similar regulated pilots?
48:31 - 49:05 Maya: We can share redacted case studies and a reference list; I'll include an intro to a couple of customers who've done quantitative signal serving with us.

49:20 - 50:00 [closing logistics]
50:01 - 50:30 Maya: We'll send the pilot scoping doc, SOC2/KMS notes, sample schema repo, and a calendar invite for the benchmark run.
50:31 - 51:10 Lena: Thanks everyone, looking forward to the pilot.
51:11 - 51:45 Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up. Bye.
51:46 - 54:00 [hangout ends, faint chatter and recording stops]
